Law of Conservation of Mass (Lavoisier): Total mass of reactants equals total mass of products in a chemical reaction.
Law of Definite Proportions (Proust): A pure compound always contains the same elements in fixed proportion by mass.
Law of Multiple Proportions (Dalton): When two elements form more than one compound, masses of one element combining with fixed mass of other are in simple whole-number ratios.

Law of Reciprocal Proportions (Richter): When two elements combine separately with a fixed mass of a third element, the ratio of their masses in which they combine with each other is either the same or a simple multiple.
Gay-Lussac's Law of Gaseous Volumes: Gases react in simple whole-number volume ratios at same temperature and pressure.
Avogadro's Law: Equal volumes of all gases at same temperature and pressure contain equal number of molecules.

summary: Overview reference for the five laws of stoichiometry. Detailed content is available in the individual concept files for each law.
examShortTricks: Trick 1: Match law to example in one line — conservation of mass: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O (mass of reactants = mass of products); definite proportions: pure water is always H2O in 1:8 ratio; multiple proportions: CO and CO2.
Trick 2: For multiple proportions, fix the mass of ONE element and compare the variable element — in CO and CO2, 12 g C combines with 16 g and 32 g O: ratio 16:32 = 1:2 (simple whole number).
Trick 3: Reciprocal proportions: two elements combining with a THIRD in simple ratios also combine with each other in simple ratios — C:H = 3:1 (CH4), H:O = 1:8 (H2O), so C:O = 3:8 (CO2).
practiceQuestions: Q. CO and CO2 illustrate which law? Show the calculation. (2 marks) — Multiple proportions: fixed 12 g C combines with 16 g O (CO) and 32 g O (CO2); 16:32 = 1:2.

Q. 1.375 g of cupric oxide gave 1.100 g Cu on reduction; 1.79 g of copper gave 2.245 g cupric oxide. Show the law illustrated. (3 marks) — Cu:O ratio is the same (≈ 4:1) in both samples → law of definite proportions.
